paras: The attempted lynching of Ed Bridges, Ben Ray and George Blakeman took place on a Sunday night in April 1882, when an armed mob of about 150 men from Strong City surrounded the Chase County jail at Cottonwood Falls, Kansas, intending to lynch three Black prisoners. Sheriff Balch had removed the men minutes earlier, and the mob fired revolvers into the air and dispersed. The men had been charged in the fatal shooting of George Babb, a white man, and the case ended with Bridges sentenced to ten years in prison and the other two freed.

On the night of April 4, 1882, the Black residents of the area held a Masonic installation, supper and dance at Strong City, following the dedication of a colored Masonic lodge at Cottonwood Falls. The Emporia Weekly News first reported that the trouble began when a Cottonwood Falls man tried to get into the dance without paying and was slapped by the doorkeeper, while a later account said Blakeman and Babb, both drunk, quarreled and Blakeman slapped Babb. In the shooting that followed, Babb, a stone mason, received two mortal wounds and died on April 8, Bridges was shot through the arm and across the breast, and Wes Walker and Deputy Sheriff Jabe Johnson were shot in the hand.

A coroner's jury found that Walker, Bridges and Ray had done the shooting, and Walker fled. Ray was arrested at Emporia, where officials already thought it unsafe to move him "for fear of mob violence."

According to "special advices from Cottonwood Falls," a mob of about 150 organized at Strong City on Sunday with the purpose of lynching Bridges, Ray, alias Scraggs, and Blakeman, who were held at Cottonwood Falls. Warned at about ten o'clock that night, Sheriff Balch procured a team and drove off with the three men, announcing the jail at Eureka in Greenwood County as his destination. Within ten minutes the mob, "armed to the teeth," surrounded the jail and called for the prisoners. Finding them gone, its members shouted imprecations, fired their revolvers into the air and eventually dispersed.

The three men were in fact lodged in the Emporia jail, where they stayed until about May 8. They were then taken back to Cottonwood Falls because "no fears of mob violence are entertained," and Ray, who had waived examination, was held on $8,000 bail. No report of arrests of mob members appears in the coverage.

In June a jury convicted Bridges of second-degree murder even though six witnesses swore he fired the first shot and six swore he was unarmed and that Babb fired first. The charge against Blakeman was dropped by nolle prosequi, a motion for a new trial for Bridges was overruled in August, and he was sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary. By December Ray had been acquitted, Bridges's attorneys had taken his case to the state supreme court, and Walker had been arrested, tried and acquitted.

The mob was reported in the Emporia Weekly News, which ran the story under the headline "DIDN'T FIND THEM IN" with the subhead "To Avenge the Murder of Babb, but Find the Prisoners Flown." The paper called the prisoners "culprits" and "birds" that had flown, yet closed by regretting that Strong City citizens should "take the law in their own hands" and hoping "better counsels" would prevail. Its later items followed the murder case closely but mentioned the mob only once more, and a Medicine Lodge paper's state-news column called Bridges "a murderer of Strong City." No coverage in the Black press, whose surviving files begin later, or in a Chase County paper beyond one item reprinted from the Chase County Leader was found.
The main April 13 story gave Eureka as the sheriff's destination, but a note in the same issue and later reports placed the prisoners in the Emporia jail.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Bridges, Ben Ray and George Blakeman
bases: An armed mob of about 150 surrounded the Chase county jail at Cottonwood Falls intending to lynch three Black prisoners, who had been removed by the sheriff minutes earlier (A2, A3).
No one was killed: the sheriff removed the prisoners before a mob of about 150 that meant 'to lynch' them reached the jail to avenge Babb's killing (A2, A3); it was an attempted lynching.
The mob is described only by the Emporia Weekly News, in its main account and a brief note in the same issue, with a later recollection (A2, A3, A5).

accounts.label: Emporia News, special advices from Cottonwood Falls
accounts.gist: A mob of about 150 organized at Strong City to lynch the three prisoners; the sheriff spirited them away, and the armed mob found the jail empty, fired revolvers in the air and dispersed.

accounts.label: Emporia News retrospective
accounts.gist: Recalled that the papers had mentioned a mob organized 'to take the prisoners out and hang them' and that the prisoners were kept in the Emporia jail till May 8.

framing.detail: The Emporia News regretted that Strong City citizens sought 'to take the law in their own hands' while calling the prisoners 'culprits' and 'birds' that had flown.
Later items followed the murder case without mention of the mob, apart from one recollection; a Medicine Lodge paper called Bridges 'a murderer of Strong City'.
